title: Philosophy of Science
availability: This course is compulsory on the BSc in Philosophy, Logic and Scientific Method. This course is available on the BSc in Philosophy and Economics, BSc in Philosophy, Politics and Economics, BSc in Philosophy, Politics and Economics (with a Year Abroad), BSc in Politics and Philosophy, Erasmus Reciprocal Programme of Study and Exchange Programme for Students from University of California, Berkeley. This course is freely available as an outside option to students on other programmes where regulations permit. It does not require permission. This course is freely available to General Course students. It does not require permission.
description: Science is chock full of miraculous predictions, shocking revolutions, and unexpected results that few science fiction writers could have ever dreamed of. What makes science so special? This course is a tour of the philosophical underpinnings of modern science. No background in any science is needed for this course; everything you need to know will be covered. Indicative topics include: the structure of science and of the philosophy of science: Popper, Lakatos, Kuhn, and beyond. Formal epistemology of science and social structures of science, including computational models of diversity and inequality (no computational background needed). Explanation and confirmation: the deductive nomological explanation, statistical explanation, hypothetic-deductive confirmation, Bayesianism. Laws of Nature: the regularity view of laws, the best systems account. Realism versus Antirealism: Scientific realism and antirealism, the no miracles argument, inference to the best explanation, the pessimistic meta-induction, constructive empiricism, entity realism, structural realism. Models: scientific modelling and scientific representation.
teaching: 10 hours of lectures and 10 hours of classes in the Autumn Term. 10 hours of lectures and 10 hours of classes in the Winter Term. This course has a reading week in Week 6 of Autumn and Winter Term.
formativeAssessment: One 1,500 word essay and in-class group work including a group presentation in AT, and one essay in WT, participation in class discussions.
indicativeReading: Theory and Reality: An Introduction to the Philosophy of Science.
Contemporary Debates in Philosophy of Science
assessmentText: Exam (50%), duration: 180 minutes in the Spring exam period. Essay (25%, 2000 words). Essay (25%, 2000 words).
